ppl-team.summary: A small, named in-house security team that owns the programme, runs the tools and manages the partners.
ppl-team.protects: Every other control: tools and contracts give no protection unless people configure, watch and improve them.
ppl-team.placement: Process owner: CISO, with HR. Sits in the second line (risk) or in IT, but reports to the CISO.
ppl-team.how: Size the team to the estate, then hire the leads first (GRC, security engineering, SOC, IR). A 24x7 watch is usually bought as a managed SOC, with an in-house manager and L2/L3 staff who own escalations. Consultants may fill gaps for a year if knowledge transfer is written into the contract.
pareto: A named CISO with a direct line to the CEO or Board risk committee
Four leads first: GRC, security engineering, SOC/IR, security testing
Buy 24x7 L1 monitoring as a managed service; keep L2/L3 and IR in-house
A written role profile, a training plan and a backup person for every key role

vendors.name: Indian IT services firms with managed security practices (for example TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech)
vendors.fit: Co-sourced SOC and staff augmentation at scale; choose when 24x7 cover is needed fast.
vendors.india: Headquartered in India; delivery centres in all metros.

vendors.name: Big Four advisory (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC India)
vendors.fit: Interim CISO, GRC and regulatory programmes for BFSI; choose for regulator-facing work.
vendors.india: Large India cyber practices in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Gurugram, Hyderabad, Pune.

vendors.name: Specialist recruiters and staffing firms (for example Taggd, which publishes India cyber salary data)
vendors.fit: Permanent hiring of security roles; useful for hard-to-fill SOC and cloud roles.

vendors.name: ISC2, ISACA and OWASP India chapters; DSCI community
vendors.fit: Not vendors but the best talent pool: chapter meetings and job boards reach certified people.

cost.unit: salary cost per person per year (CTC)
cost.band: Rs 4-10 lakh (SOC L1), Rs 7-18 lakh (engineer), Rs 15-30 lakh (BFSI specialist at 4-6 years), Rs 40 lakh-1 crore+ (CISO)
cost.reference_org: an in-house core of about 10-14 people (with L1 monitoring bought as a managed SOC) costs roughly Rs 2-4 crore a year in salary; a fully in-house 24x7 SOC adds about five people per seat watched around the clock
cost.note: Salary bands are from 2026 India salary surveys and career blogs, not an authoritative pay report; check with two recruiters. indicative; get three quotes

scope: Staff augmentation or co-sourcing for named roles
24x7 L1 monitoring if bought as a service
Knowledge transfer to named internal staff
Background verification of all deployed staff
must: Named resources with CVs approved by the organisation before deployment
Replacement of a departing resource within 30 days, with a 2-week overlap
Certifications as stated per role (for example CISSP, CISM, OSCP, GCIH)
Police and employment background checks for every person
should: Bench strength in the same city
Resources who have worked in RBI- or SEBI-regulated entities
A training budget per resource paid by the provider
sizing: 24x7 cover: how many seats around the clock
Expected growth in users and applications over 3 years
sla: Attrition below 20% a year for deployed staff
clauses: RBI IT outsourcing directions: the regulated entity keeps accountability; right to audit the provider
Confidentiality and non-disclosure for every resource
Non-solicitation in both directions, with a buy-out fee
Exit and transition: handover of all documents, credentials and runbooks

ppl-team.architecture: The CISO heads three or four leads. The SOC manager runs the managed SOC contract and the in-house L2/L3 analysts. The GRC lead owns policy, risk and audits. Engineering owns the security tools. IR leads incidents with the SOC. HR owns hiring, training budget and succession.
kpis: Open critical roles and days to fill
Percentage of key roles with a trained backup
Annual attrition in the security team
Percentage of tools with a named owner
pitfalls: Buying tools before hiring the people to run them
A one-person team with no backup
Consultants doing the work with no knowledge transfer
Paying below BFSI market rates and losing staff within a year

ppl-awareness.summary: Short, regular security lessons for every employee plus fake phishing tests that show who needs more help.
ppl-awareness.protects: People and the accounts, money and data they can reach; against phishing, payment fraud, smishing, vishing and social engineering.
ppl-awareness.placement: Cloud service (SaaS platform) run by the CISO's team, with HR and communications. Integrates with the e-mail system and the directory.
ppl-awareness.how: The platform sends short lessons each month and simulated phishing e-mails, SMS or calls each quarter. It records who clicked, who reported, and who finished training. People who click get a short lesson at once; repeat clickers get one-to-one help.
pareto: A one-click 'report phishing' button, with feedback to the reporter
Quarterly phishing simulations with instant teachable moments
Extra training for high-risk groups: finance, treasury, executives, helpdesk
Lessons in local languages and on payment-fraud scenarios
Report rate tracked, not only click rate

vendors.fit: Largest content library and simulation templates; choose for breadth and mature reporting.

Reported real phish go to the SOC mailbox. Results feed the GRC tool and the Board dashboard.
kpis: Phishing click rate (target below 5%)
Report rate (target above 60%)
Training completion within 30 days (target above 95%)
Time from first report to SOC action
pitfalls: Measuring only clicks and shaming people, which stops them reporting
Once-a-year compliance video that changes nothing
No allow-listing, so simulations land in spam and results are false
No extra help for high-risk roles

ppl-training.summary: A training and certification plan for each security role, with a budget per person per year.
ppl-training.protects: The team's skills, and so the quality of every control they run; reduces reliance on consultants.
ppl-training.placement: Process owner: CISO with HR (learning and development).
ppl-training.how: Each role has a list of skills and one target certification. Each person gets a yearly budget, study time and a plan agreed at appraisal. Hands-on labs and a range keep skills current between courses.
pareto: One relevant certification per person per year, tied to the role
Hands-on lab subscriptions rather than slides
Study time in work hours, protected in the roster
A retention bond for expensive courses

ppl-kt.summary: A written plan that makes every consultant leave skills, documents and runbooks behind, so the internal team can take over.
ppl-kt.protects: The organisation's independence and continuity; against lock-in, loss of knowledge when a contract ends, and paying twice for the same work.
ppl-kt.placement: Process owner: CISO, enforced through procurement and each consulting contract.
ppl-kt.how: Each consulting statement of work names the internal shadow for each deliverable, the documents to hand over and a sign-off test. In year 1 the consultant leads and the staff shadow; in year 2 the staff lead and the consultant reviews. Payment milestones depend on accepted knowledge transfer.
pareto: A named internal shadow for every consultant role
Runbooks, configurations and credentials handed over in a shared wiki
Reverse shadowing: staff do the task while the consultant watches
Part of the fee held back until KT sign-off

vendors.name: Big Four advisory (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC India)
vendors.fit: Typical source of consultants; ask for a KT plan with named milestones.

vendors.name: Indian IT services and security specialists (for example TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and CERT-In empanelled firms)
vendors.fit: Deliver managed services and projects; KT and exit plans must be in the contract.

vendors.name: Atlassian Confluence or Microsoft SharePoint
vendors.fit: The wiki where runbooks and KT records live; use what the organisation already has.
vendors.india: Cloud regions or partners in India.

vendors.name: MkDocs, Wiki.js or Moodle (learning records)
vendors.fit: Free wiki and learning tools for runbooks and short KT courses.

cost.band: Rs 0 extra in licence; the KT effort is built into each consulting contract
cost.reference_org: no separate budget line; ask bidders to price KT as a separate, visible milestone
drivers: how much shadow time staff can give
complexity of the systems handed over
cost.note: No product price applies. Our own advice, not a sourced figure: make KT a priced milestone so it is not cut. indicative; get three quotes

scope: Runbooks, design documents and configuration exports
must: KT plan submitted within 30 days of start
Named internal shadow for each consultant
All runbooks and configuration in the organisation's own wiki and repository
Sign-off by the internal owner before final payment
should: A short quiz or practical task for each shadow
sizing: Number of systems and processes to hand over
Number of internal staff to be trained
sla: Runbook for each managed system within 60 days
KT sessions as scheduled, at least 95% held
Hand-over complete within the exit period
clauses: RBI IT outsourcing directions: exit strategy and orderly transition to the organisation or a new provider
Ownership of all documents and work products by the organisation
Holdback of part of the fee until KT sign-off
Configuration escrow or export of all settings at exit

ppl-kt.architecture: Procurement adds the KT schedule to every statement of work. The CISO's PMO tracks KT milestones. Runbooks live in the internal wiki; configurations in the internal repository. HR records new skills in the skills matrix.
kpis: Percentage of consulting deliverables with signed KT
Consultant days reduced year on year
Systems with an internal runbook owner
Successful operation by internal staff during a consultant's absence
pitfalls: KT left to the last week of the contract
Documents kept in the consultant's own systems
No internal person free to shadow
Paying in full before KT is accepted

ppl-range.summary: Realistic practice attacks in a safe copy of an IT environment, so the team rehearses detection and response.
ppl-range.protects: Response speed and quality: the SOC, IR and IT teams who must act during a real attack.
ppl-range.placement: Isolated lab or cloud service, owned by the SOC manager; never connected to production.
ppl-range.how: The range runs a scenario (for example ransomware or a phishing-led breach) in a virtual network. The team detects, contains and reports, while the range scores time and decisions. A debrief turns gaps into fixes and training.
pareto: Quarterly exercises built on your own top threats
Use the same tools as production (SIEM, EDR) where possible
A timed debrief with actions owned and tracked
Include the regulator reporting step (CERT-In 6 hours) in the scenario

prc-vuln.summary: A repeating cycle that finds weaknesses, ranks them, gets them fixed within agreed deadlines and checks the fix.
prc-vuln.protects: Servers, endpoints, network devices, applications and cloud; against attackers using known flaws.
prc-vuln.placement: Process owner: security testing lead. Scanners sit on the internal network and in the cloud, with agents on endpoints; fixes are done by IT and application owners.
prc-vuln.how: Scanners and agents find flaws every week; external tests and VAPT add depth. Each finding is rated by severity, exploitation (CISA KEV, EPSS) and asset criticality, then assigned to an owner with a deadline. A re-scan or re-test closes it; overdue items are escalated.
pareto: A complete asset list that the scanner covers (unknown assets are never fixed)
Fix known-exploited flaws (CISA KEV) first, within days
Clear closure deadlines by severity, agreed by IT and the business
Re-test before closing, and a monthly overdue report to the CIO

vendors.name: Tenable (Nessus, Tenable Vulnerability Management)
vendors.fit: Very wide plug-in coverage; strong for mixed estates.

vendors.name: Qualys VMDR
vendors.fit: Cloud-based scanning with agents and patching add-ons; widely used by Indian banks.
vendors.india: Large engineering centre in Pune; Indian cloud platform option should be confirmed.

vendors.fit: Good dashboards and remediation projects.

vendors.name: Greenbone OpenVAS
vendors.fit: Free network scanner; needs more tuning and staff time.

vendors.fit: Independent VA/PT required by regulators; RBI expects VA every 6 months and PT every 12 months for critical systems.
vendors.india: Indian firms; list on the CERT-In site.

cost.note: Third-party 2026 estimates: Tenable about USD 26-38, Qualys about USD 17-40, Rapid7 about USD 25 per asset per year. The scanner licence is counted under tec-vulnscan in govern.json. USD list prices converted at about Rs 84/USD; excludes 18% GST. indicative; get three quotes

Half-yearly VA and yearly PT of critical systems by an independent firm

CISA KEV and EPSS shown for each finding
Ticket integration (ServiceNow, Jira or the ITSM in use)
Re-scan to confirm closure
Scan data stored in India or on-premises
should: Agent for laptops off the network
sizing: 2,500 endpoints, about 300-500 servers and network devices (confirm)
sla: Critical and KEV: fix within 7 days (internet-facing within 72 hours)
clauses: RBI IT governance directions: VA at least every 6 months and PT every 12 months for critical and DMZ systems, by independent experts
CERT-In empanelled auditor for regulatory audits
Confidentiality of findings; no copies kept by the auditor beyond the retention period
Right to audit the scanning vendor

prc-vuln.architecture: The asset inventory feeds the scanner. Scanners in each site and the cloud, plus agents on endpoints, send results to the console. The console feeds tickets to the ITSM and risk scores to the SIEM and the GRC dashboard. Patch management fixes most findings.
kpis: Percentage of assets scanned in the last 7 days
Mean time to remediate by severity
Open KEV findings older than 7 days (target zero)
Repeat findings across scans
pitfalls: Unauthenticated scans that miss most flaws
Ranking by CVSS alone and drowning in 'critical' items
Closing tickets without a re-scan
Assets missing from the scanner's scope

prc-patch.summary: A planned monthly cycle, plus an emergency path, for installing security updates on every device and system.
prc-patch.protects: Endpoints, servers, network devices and applications; against attacks on flaws that already have a fix.
prc-patch.placement: Process owner: IT operations. A patch tool with agents on devices, a central console in the data centre or cloud, and change management approval.
prc-patch.how: Patches are tested on a small pilot group, then deployed in rings across the estate within a set window. Flaws in CISA's KEV list, or under active attack, take the emergency path within days. A weekly coverage report shows which devices are missing patches.
pareto: One tool that covers the operating system and the top third-party apps (browsers, PDF, Java)
Deployment rings: pilot, early, broad
An emergency path for exploited flaws, pre-approved in change management
A weekly compliance report by site and owner
A list of end-of-support systems with a replacement plan

Reports that show deployment, not installation

prc-access.summary: Granting access only when needed, changing it when people move, removing it the day they leave, and reviewing it every quarter.
prc-access.protects: Accounts and data in critical systems; against leftover access, insider misuse and attackers using old accounts.
prc-access.placement: Process owners: IT and HR. HR is the source of joiners, movers and leavers; an identity governance tool or the ITSM carries the workflow.
prc-access.how: HR events start account creation, change or removal automatically. Each quarter, managers and application owners confirm who still needs access to critical systems; anything not confirmed is removed. Privileged and service accounts get a tighter, monthly review.
pareto: HR feed drives leaver removal on the same day
Quarterly reviews of critical and payment systems
Monthly review of privileged and service accounts
Removal of dormant accounts after 90 days

prc-ir.summary: A written, practised plan that says who does what in a cyber incident and in a wider crisis, including reporting to regulators on time.
prc-ir.protects: Operations, customers and reputation; limits damage from ransomware, breaches and fraud, and meets the CERT-In 6-hour clock.
prc-ir.placement: Process owner: IR lead, with the CISO, legal, communications and business heads. Works with the SOC and an external IR retainer firm.
prc-ir.how: The plan defines severity levels, roles, a contact tree and playbooks for the main threats. It names who reports to CERT-In within 6 hours and to RBI or SEBI as required. A retainer firm gives forensic help on call, and tabletop exercises test the plan twice a year.
pareto: Playbooks for ransomware, business e-mail compromise, data leak and payment fraud
A regulator-reporting checklist (CERT-In 6 hours; RBI, SEBI, DPDP Board as applicable)
An IR retainer signed before it is needed
An out-of-band contact tree and communication channel
Logs kept 180 days in India, so forensics is possible

prc-backup.summary: Copies of important data and systems kept in several places, at least one offline or immutable, and restored on a schedule to prove they work.
prc-backup.protects: Business data and systems; against ransomware, deletion, corruption and site loss.
prc-backup.placement: Process owner: IT operations. Backup servers in the data centre, a copy at the DR site, and an immutable or offline copy (tape, object lock or a vault).
prc-backup.how: Follow 3-2-1-1-0: three copies, two media types, one off-site, one offline or immutable, and zero errors after restore tests. Backup credentials are separate from the main directory. Restores are tested every quarter and the critical systems are restored in full once a year.
pareto: An immutable or offline copy that admins cannot delete
Backup system accounts separate from Active Directory, with MFA
Quarterly restore tests that open the data, not only checksums
Encryption of backups at rest and in transit
Backup of SaaS data (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) too

prc-sdlc.summary: Building security into each software release: requirements, threat modelling, secure coding, testing and an API checklist before go-live.

prc-sdlc.how: Each new feature gets security requirements (OWASP ASVS) and a short threat model. Code and dependencies are scanned in the pipeline, and APIs are tested against a checklist. A release with open critical findings does not go live without a signed exception.

Dependency (SCA) and secret scanning in every build

prc-drills.summary: Regular rehearsals of business continuity and disaster recovery, plus discussion-based tabletop exercises with management.
prc-drills.protects: Critical services and their recovery times; against site loss, ransomware, outages and confused decision-making in a crisis.
prc-drills.placement: Process owner: resilience lead (BCM), with IT operations, business heads and the CISO.

prc-ctem.summary: A continuous programme that keeps finding, ranking, testing and fixing the exposures attackers could actually use.
prc-ctem.protects: The whole attack surface: internet-facing assets, identities, cloud, endpoints and third-party exposure.
prc-ctem.placement: Process owner: CISO. Uses exposure-management, attack-surface and validation tools in the cloud and on the network; fixes go to IT and application owners.
prc-ctem.how: Gartner's CTEM model runs five stages in a loop: scope, discover, prioritise, validate and mobilise. Tools combine scanner, identity and cloud data into attack paths; validation (breach simulation or testing) proves which ones work. Monthly cycles hand a short, proven fix list to owners.
pareto: Scope by business service, starting with internet-facing and payment systems
Combine vulnerability, identity and cloud data into attack paths
Validate the top exposures before asking owners to fix them
A short monthly fix list with business owners, not a long scan report
